candidates.label: Migdal (Majdal)
candidates.support: The Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire's point sits within about 250 meters of OpenBible.info's independently recorded point for the same village, but roughly 1.6-2.3 km from the points recorded on two separate Wikidata items describing the ancient site and the modern town, a spread consistent with genuine uncertainty over the precise center of the ancient settlement within the wider modern-town area rather than a firmly resolved single point.

summary.text: Magdala, on the western shore of the Sea of Galilee near Tiberias, is best known as the home village implied by the epithet 'Magdalene' given to Mary Magdalene throughout the Gospels; a place named Magadan or Dalmanutha in the same general area is also mentioned in Matthew and Mark.

history.text: Excavations beginning in 2009 uncovered a first-century synagogue together with a paved street and a building resting against a stone quay on the ancient shoreline, consistent with the description given by the first-century Jewish historian Josephus of the town, which he calls Taricheae, as a fishing and fish-processing center on the lake.

scripture.textWEB: Then he sent away the multitudes, got into the boat, and came into the borders of Magdala.
Immediately he entered into the boat with his disciples and came into the region of Dalmanutha.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Tetrarchy of Galilee and Perea (ruler: Herod Antipas)
Kingdom of Herod Agrippa I (ruler: Herod Agrippa I)

politicalHistory.note: The emperor Nero later added the Galilean towns of Tiberias and Taricheae (identified with Magdala), and Julias in Perea with fourteen villages, to Agrippa II's kingdom; the Jewish historian Josephus dates this to AD 54, but the Jewish Encyclopedia (1906) reads Agrippa II's coinage as pointing to AD 61 instead. These are towns, not land of their own, so this area's extent does not change.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod Agrippa II (ruler: Herod Agrippa II)
politicalHistory.note: The Jewish historian Josephus records that the emperor Nero gave Agrippa II "a certain part of Galilee, Tiberias, and Tarichae," naming this town by its other name; Josephus dates the grant to Nero's first year (AD 54), but the Jewish Encyclopedia (1906) reads Agrippa II's own coinage as pointing to AD 61 instead for this specific addition. The rest of Galilee stayed under the Roman procurators throughout.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Legates, with a legion now based at Jerusalem)
politicalHistory.note: An administrative upgrade (a legate instead of a procurator), not a border or name change.
